tool.name: CountsShares
tool.summary: Builds an egocentric neighbourhood around EVERY point and counts what is inside it. Two ways to draw it: k (the nearest k persons - population fixed, radius floats, reported as Dist_k) or a radius in metres (area fixed, population floats). Group fields add counts and shares (T_ and R_). Barriers and terrain turn plain distance into EFFORT: rivers, railways, lakes, friction rasters and slopes make neighbours farther away in rounds, and N_tau### counts who is reachable within a budget. Inputs may be point layers (geometry is read directly) or tables with coordinate columns; coordinates must be metric.

param.name: layer
param.displayname: Input points (layer) or table
param.dialogReference: The points to analyse - a point layer (coordinates are read straight from the geometry) or a plain table with coordinate columns. Coordinates must be metric; degree data is refused unless auto-projection is ticked.

param.name: coordsrc
param.displayname: Coordinate source
param.dialogReference: Auto uses the geometry when the input has any, and attribute fields otherwise. Choose Attribute fields to override, e.g. when a layer carries coordinates in columns you trust more than its geometry.

param.name: xfield
param.displayname: X field (easting) - tables/attribute mode
param.dialogReference: The easting column - only for tables or attribute mode. Guessed when the name is recognisable (X/East/Easting/POINT_X...); no renaming is needed.

param.name: yfield
param.displayname: Y field (northing) - tables/attribute mode
param.dialogReference: The northing column - only for tables or attribute mode.

param.name: refmode
param.displayname: How is the reference population defined?
param.dialogReference: How the reference population is built, from the simplest way upward. 'Every point counts as one' needs nothing else - one row, one thing. 'A field holds the count' is for rows that stand for several people (or guests, or dwellings). 'Only selected types' is for a layer holding many kinds of object where only some belong: eating places among all POIs, say. Boxes that the chosen way does not need are greyed out.

param.name: pop
param.displayname: Count field - how many people (or guests, jobs, dwellings) each row stands for
param.dialogReference: How many each point stands for - people, jobs, dwellings, services, anything countable. Leave empty when every point counts as one. k counts these, so this field decides how far the k-search must travel - and in Value Statistics every statistic is weighted by it, so a point standing for 40 counts 40 times a point standing for one.

param.name: catfield
param.displayname: Type field - the column holding the kind of each object (POI type, tenure, country of birth...)
param.dialogReference: Build population and groups from the VALUES of one column (codes or names both work) instead of count fields.

param.name: reftable
param.displayname: Types to INCLUDE in the reference population - one per row, picked from the type field's own values
param.dialogReference: Which values of the category field belong to the REFERENCE population - the people or places whose k nearest form each neighbourhood. Leave it EMPTY and every row belongs. This one choice decides what your shares are shares OF: list the eating places and 'fast food' is measured against eating places; leave it empty and the same run measures fast food against every point in the layer.

param.name: keepoutside
param.displayname: Rows whose type is NOT included
param.dialogReference: What happens to a row whose type you did NOT include - a library, when the reference population is eating places. 'Give them results, counting as zero' (the default): the library is nobody's neighbour and changes no one else's numbers, but it still gets its own results, so you can ask what is around the library. 'Leave their results Null': the row is dropped from the run entirely. Note that a row you DID include whose count field is empty behaves like the first case anyway - zero people, still gets results.

param.name: treatmode
param.displayname: How is the treatment population defined?
param.dialogReference: How the treatment population is built - the thing you count inside each neighbourhood. 'Not measuring one' is a real answer: you then get N and Dist_k alone, which is how far away the k nearest are. 'One column per group' suits data with a column of counts per group. 'Types from a type field' suits a labelled column, and you say which labels form which group. There is no count field here: k belongs to the reference population, so the treatment is counted in the same units and every share sits between 0 and 1.

param.name: treatcatfield
param.displayname: Type field for the groups (often the same column as above - choose it here too)
param.dialogReference: The column holding the type of each object, for building the groups. Usually the same column the reference population used - choose it here as well, so this section reads on its own.

param.name: treattable
param.displayname: Groups: one row per type - the type, and the group name it joins. Rows sharing a group name merge.
param.dialogReference: Which values form which GROUP in the treatment population - the thing you are counting inside each neighbourhood. One row per value: the value, and the name of the group it joins. Rows sharing a group name merge, so 'restaurant', 'cafe' and 'pub' can all become 'eating'. You get a T_ column (the count) and an R_ column (its share of the reference population) for each group.

param.name: restgroup
param.displayname: Name a group for every OTHER type (optional; for example: other)
param.dialogReference: Optional. Name only the values you care about in the table above, then type a name here - say 'other' - and EVERY remaining value of the category field joins that group automatically. With 130 POI types this is the difference between five rows and a hundred and thirty.

param.name: treat
param.displayname: Group count fields - one column per group, holding how many of that group each row stands for (TOTALS, not averages)
param.dialogReference: Group counts: persons of the group at this point (use 0/1 when points are individuals). Produces T_<group>_k (count) and R_<group>_k (share). These columns are ADDED UP across the neighbourhood, so give TOTALS, never averages: total income at this point, not mean income per person here. A per-point average belongs in tool 2 (Value Statistics), which weights it by the reference population instead of summing it.

param.name: k
param.displayname: k values (space-separated, e.g. 200 1600)
param.dialogReference: One or more k values, space-separated (200 1600). Each k gives its own neighbourhood: the nearest k PERSONS, so the radius floats and Dist_k reports it.

param.name: r
param.displayname: Radii in metres (e.g. 500 1000)
param.dialogReference: Fixed radii in metres, space-separated. The mirror image of k: the area is fixed and the population floats (N_r###).

param.name: model
param.displayname: Distance decay
param.dialogReference: Distance decay weighting. 'no decay' counts every neighbour equally inside the neighbourhood.

param.name: halflife
param.displayname: Decay half-life in metres (one value for everybody)
param.dialogReference: The distance in metres at which a neighbour counts half as much. Only used when a decay model is chosen.

param.name: hlfield
param.displayname: OR: half-life from a field - each point keeps its own bandwidth (estimated median distance, group potential...)
param.dialogReference: A field giving each point its OWN half-life in metres - an estimated median travel distance, a group-specific potential, whatever you have estimated. Rows are grouped into bandwidth bins and each bin gets its own exact pass.

param.name: hlfromdist
param.displayname: OR: self-calibrating - use each point's own Dist_k as its half-life (enter the k to calibrate on; urban form sets the bandwidth)
param.dialogReference: Self-calibrating bandwidth: enter a k, and each point's own Dist_k - the radius it needed to gather k persons - becomes its half-life. Dense places get sharp kernels, thin places broad ones, with no external estimate.

param.name: hlbins
param.displayname: Bandwidth bins (variable half-life only; more bins = finer, slower)
param.dialogReference: How many bandwidth bins to use when the half-life varies. More bins follow the distribution more closely and cost more passes; distinct values fewer than this get an exact pass each.

param.name: decayeps
param.displayname: Decay cutoff - ignore weights below this (smaller = wider search = slower; the truncation distance is reported in the messages)
param.dialogReference: Where the decayed sum is cut off: neighbours whose weight falls below this are ignored. A decayed sum has no natural edge, so this is what bounds the search. 1e-6 (the default) reaches about 20 half-lives and is slow; 1e-3 reaches about 10 and runs roughly four times faster, with a difference far below any sampling error. The actual distance in metres is reported in the messages.

param.name: barriertable
param.displayname: Barriers: one row per point/line/polygon layer or table of cells, with the field holding its friction
param.dialogReference: One row per barrier source - a point, line or polygon layer, or a table of cells - with the field holding its friction. Friction is a DELAY, not a distance: entering a cell costs 1 + friction, so 3 is a river (four rounds), 0 is open ground, and a NEGATIVE value down to -1 is a facilitator - -0.9 makes a cell a tenth of a round, which is how a motorway is modelled. -1 and below are refused. Several sources combine per the overlap rule, so a river, a railway and a lake can be given together.

param.name: barrierrasters
param.displayname: Barrier rasters (cell value = friction); combined with the rows above by the same overlap rule
param.dialogReference: Friction rasters, where each cell value is the crossing cost - positive deters, negative carries, and -1 is the refused floor. They combine with the rows of the barrier table by the same overlap rule.

param.name: barrieragg
param.displayname: Barrier overlap rule (features sharing a cell)
param.dialogReference: How several barrier features sharing one cell combine. Additive (the default) stacks costs - a river crossed at a railway costs both. Max/min/mean are available when stacking is wrong.

param.name: dem
param.displayname: Distance ingredient: elevation raster (DEM)
param.dialogReference: Elevation raster: slopes become extra effort, so uphill neighbours are farther away than flat ones.

param.name: tau
param.displayname: Effort budgets in rounds (e.g. 3 8)
param.dialogReference: Effort budgets in rounds, space-separated. With barriers or terrain, N_tau### counts the persons reachable within that many rounds instead of within a plain radius.

param.name: roundtrip
param.displayname: Round trip (journey home included)
param.dialogReference: Count the journey home as well - the budget must cover getting there AND back.

param.name: existing
param.displayname: If result fields already exist
param.dialogReference: What to do when result fields of the same name are already present: overwrite them, or stop.

param.name: outmode
param.dialogReference: Append results to the input layer, or write a new feature class (recommended for shapefiles: a file geodatabase has no 10-character field-name limit).

param.name: outfc
param.displayname: New feature class (name/path)
param.dialogReference: Path and name of the new feature class. Put it in a file geodatabase to keep full-length result names - shapefile field names are capped at 10 characters.

param.name: outtable
param.displayname: Output table (.csv) - for TABLE inputs
param.dialogReference: Where a TABLE input's results are written (.csv). The output carries your coordinates plus the result columns, in the original row order.

param.name: unit
param.displayname: Cell size (m)
param.dialogReference: The grid cell size in metres. Bigger cells mean fewer origins and much faster runs; smaller cells mean finer geography. This is the strongest speed control you have.

param.name: selfpot
param.displayname: Self-potential - how far away your OWN cell's people are (0 = at the centre with you, as before 1.29.5; 1 = spread evenly over the cell)
param.dialogReference: Self-potential: how far away the people in your OWN cell are. They are not standing on top of you, but up to and including 1.29.3 they were treated as if they were. That mattered wherever a single cell already held k people - a dense block, a large cell - because the radius came out as zero and k stopped making any difference: the nearest 100 and the nearest 1000 gave the same answer. Leave this at 1 and their distance is estimated by spreading them evenly over the cell, which recovers the radius you would have measured from individual points to within a fraction of a percent. Set it to 0.71 for the median distance instead of the radius, or to 0 to reproduce results from 1.29.3 and earlier exactly.

param.name: autoproj
param.displayname: Auto-project degree data to a suitable metric CRS (layers only - the fitting UTM zone is computed from the data; input untouched)
param.dialogReference: When the input is in degrees, project it on the fly to the metric CRS that fits the data (the UTM zone is computed from the extent). The stored data is not modified. Tables cannot be auto-projected.

param.name: shortnames
param.displayname: Allow shortened field names when the target is a shapefile (10-character cap; names stay collision-free and the mapping is printed)
param.dialogReference: Allow result names to be shortened to 10 characters so they fit a shapefile. Names stay unique - no two results ever merge - and the full mapping is printed in the messages.

param.name: seed
param.displayname: Random seed (only matters where permutations are used; recorded in the manifest)
param.dialogReference: Seed for the parts of EquiPop that use permutations. The counting engines are deterministic; this is recorded in the run manifest so a pseudo-p-value can be reproduced.

tool.usage: Start simple: input layer, one k, nothing else. Add group fields for shares. Add a barrier layer only when barriers matter - it switches the run to the effort engine and takes longer. Cell size is the speed control: doubling it quarters the number of origins. Long result names need a roomy target: shapefile field names cap at 10 characters, so a file geodatabase is the safer home for them.
